# Taiwan
Taiwan’s education system is deeply rooted in historical influences from Dutch, Ming, Qing, and Japanese rule, with early academies promoting Confucian and Christian education. After 1949, the Republic of China centralized education under state control, initially suppressing private schools before allowing their revival under state oversight. Public education is compulsory from primary through junior high (since 1968), with a 12-year program introduced in 2011 and fully implemented since 2014, enhancing access and equity. Students take national exams for high school and university admission, choosing between liberal arts, science, or one of six vocational fields. Core subjects include Mandarin, math, science, social studies, arts, and physical education. School assignment is based on residence, leading to strategic household registration.
Higher education is nearly universal (over 95% of graduates enter university since 2008), with a system resembling the U.S. Public universities like National Taiwan University and National Tsing Hua are research-intensive and highly regarded. Private institutions such as Fu Jen Catholic and Soochow University offer specialized programs, particularly in engineering, supported by government investment in high-tech industries. University life is generally relaxed, with many graduates pursuing foreign graduate studies. Medical education spans six years with clinical training. The Teaching Excellence Universities Award recognizes top institutions for teaching quality. Military discipline oversees senior high education, with mandatory military training. Vocational education spans associate to doctoral degrees through junior colleges, institutes of technology, and universities of science and technology, emphasizing practical skills. Specialized programs include law, teacher training, and nursing, with teacher education differentiated by institution type. A nationwide digital platform supports teacher in-service education.

# Nigeria
Nigeria follows a 6-3-3-4 structure: six years of primary (age 5), three years of junior secondary, three years of senior secondary, and four years of tertiary education. Universal Basic Education (UBE, introduced in 1999) provides free, compulsory, and continuous schooling for nine years (primary + junior secondary), monitored by the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC). Core subjects in primary include Mathematics, English, Religious Knowledge, Agricultural Science, and one indigenous language (Hausa, Yoruba, or Igbo). Students pass a Common Entrance Examination to enter secondary school. In senior secondary, core subjects include English, Mathematics, Economics, and Civic Education, with electives based on academic track (science, vocational, arts). The Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE), administered by WAEC and NECO, is the primary exam for university admission, requiring seven subjects including English and Mathematics. Alternative exams like the GCE (October/November) are also offered.
School types vary: federal schools are government-funded, merit-based, and elite; state schools are state-funded but face teacher shortages and low qualifications; private/religious schools are expensive (up to 30 million naira), with smaller classes and better-trained teachers. Advanced-level programs such as the Interim Joint Matriculation Board (IJMB) and Joint University Matriculation Examination Board (JUPEB) enable direct entry into university. As of 2021, 99 universities are approved by the Nigeria University Commission (NUC), including 9 new private universities. Universities are categorized into three generations: first (1948–1965), second (1970–1985), and third (1980–1990), with a focus on technology and agriculture. Undergraduate programs last 3–6 years (e.g., 4 years for Humanities, 6 for Medicine). Entry requires SSCE credits and a JAMB score of 180+ or direct entry via NCE/ND. Vocational education is managed by the National Board for Technical Education, facing challenges in teacher shortages, outdated curricula, and labor market misalignment. Key challenges include low teacher qualifications, rising private school fees, and persistent disparities in female and rural education.

# Iran
Iran’s education system evolved from Pahlavi-era reforms to a highly centralized, Islamized structure after the 1979 revolution. Key developments include the Literacy Corps (1969–1979), which boosted literacy, and gender segregation in schools. The system is centralized under the Ministry of Education, with free public schooling and mandatory service or tuition for graduates. Despite high investment—20% of government spending and 5% of GDP—dropout rates remain high. The structure spans pre-primary to university, with university access via the competitive Konkur exam. Notable universities include Tehran, Sharif, and Amirkabir. Iran has expanded technical and vocational programs and introduced hybrid learning through Payame Noor University, though internet access remains limited in rural areas. English dominates foreign language education, with French added in 2022 to reduce English monopoly. Teacher shortages persist (over 30,000 counselors, 60,000 teachers missing). Private schools are increasingly favored, with costs up to 50 million toman per year. Women now constitute over 70% of university students, reflecting decades of progress in access and participation. The National Organization for Development of Exceptional Talents (NODET) runs selective schools for gifted students. Iran ranks among global leaders in female enrollment in primary education, engineering, and STEM graduates.

# Republic of Ireland
Education in Ireland is primarily in English, with Irish as the main language in Gaelscoileanna and a core subject in all public schools. Compulsory education spans ages 6 to 16. Primary education (8 years) includes Junior/Senior Infants to Sixth Class. Secondary education includes a three-year Junior Cycle (culminating in the Junior Certificate) and a two-year Senior Cycle (leading to the Leaving Certificate), with an optional Transition Year. Religious ethos influences school governance, though reforms have increased multi- and non-denominational options. Free preschool is available under the Early Childcare and Education Scheme. Ireland ranks highly in international assessments, especially in reading. The system emphasizes breadth and prepares students for further education or work. Special needs education is supported by the *Education for Persons with Special Educational Needs Act 2004* , with individualized programs, dyslexia support, and Special Needs Assistants (SNAs). Programs like DEIS provide resources to disadvantaged schools (over 1,200 schools by 2022), with financial aid including exam fee exemptions and remote boarding grants. Ireland ranks among the top 20 globally for education and attracts international students.

text:
# Turkey
Turkey’s education system has expanded from 5 to 12 years of compulsory education (1997–2012), enhancing access and equity. Pre-primary education is optional (ages 3–6), with 256,400 children educated in 2001–2002. Primary education spans 8 years (ages 6–14), compulsory and free in public schools. Core subjects include Turkish, math, life knowledge (replaced by science/social studies in Grade 4), and English. Secondary education includes three years after primary, with tracks in general (high schools, Anatolian, science, arts) and vocational/technical schools. Students take standardized exams and receive a standard diploma (since 2011). A new "4+4+4" system (4 years primary, 4 years middle, 4 years secondary) was introduced in 2012, including general and religious (Imam Hatip) middle schools. Higher education includes 167 universities (public and private), with public institutions offering low-cost education and private ones being expensive. Turkish universities are internationally recognized, especially in engineering (ABET-accredited), and have growing international student numbers (795,962 in 2016). Private schools include Turkish, minority, foreign, and international institutions. Religious education was reintroduced in 1956 and now includes secular and global content from 4th grade onward. The system emphasizes accessibility, affordability, and internationalization, though it faces criticism for ideological influence, curriculum bias, and poor textbook quality.

text:
# Israel
Israel places a strong societal value on education, rooted in historical Jewish emphasis on scholarship. The Israeli Pupils’ Rights Law (2000) prohibits sectarian discrimination. The matriculation exam (bagrut) is critical for university admission, military service, and employment, with high pass rates (61.5% in 2014). The education system supports a science- and technology-driven economy, with 46% of 25–64-year-olds holding tertiary degrees—second only to Japan in OECD rankings. Israel spends 7.3% of GDP on education. Higher education includes top-ranked institutions like Tel Aviv University, Hebrew University, and the Technion, with strong performance in science and engineering. Arab students have seen significant enrollment growth, though they face structural barriers including underfunding, higher dropout rates, and inferior infrastructure. Gender disparities persist: women outperform men in retention and enrollment, yet men dominate STEM and hold 81% of professorships. Teacher wages are low, and reforms face union resistance. Textbooks have been criticized for promoting negative Arab stereotypes. Labor strikes in schools and universities reflect ongoing tensions over tuition, pay, and curriculum.

text:
# France
Napoleon and Jules Ferry laid the foundation for modern French education, emphasizing secularism, mandatory, and free public schooling. Compulsory education spans ages 6 to 16, with breaks in October, December, February, April, and summer. Primary education begins at age 3 with preschool, followed by 5 years of elementary school. Middle school (collège) covers ages 11–15, and high school (lycée) prepares students for the baccalauréat or vocational training. Private schools are either "under contract" (following national curriculum) or operate independently with religious instruction. France has 105 international schools offering English-medium curricula. Higher education includes two types of private institutions: free private colleges (Facultés Libres) and Catholic Institutes (non-profit, EESPIG-qualified), and technical private colleges (e.g., HEC Paris, ESSEC). Private institutions cannot award national degrees but may offer co-diplomas or accredited diplomas. CPGEs (preparatory classes) prepare students for Grande Écoles: scientific (TSI, MPSI), business (ECS/ECE), and humanities (Hypokhâgne/Khâgne). Colles are mandatory oral exams, highly stressful but crucial for exam preparation. Teacher recruitment includes primary (Bac+5, INSPE), secondary (CAPES or Agrégés), and research-teachers (doctorate, HDR). Public schools are secular ( *laïcité* ), with religious symbols banned (2004 ruling), sparking debate over religious freedom.

# Sri Lanka
Sri Lanka’s system blends traditional Buddhist values with colonial-era reforms, with English as a key language of instruction. The system includes primary, junior secondary, senior secondary, collegiate, and tertiary levels. Primary (Grades 1–5) is followed by middle school (6–9), then senior secondary (10–11), preparing students for G.C.E. Ordinary Level (O/L) exams. Students may pursue a two-year collegiate level (12–13) leading to G.C.E. Advanced Level (A/L), the university entrance exam. Government schools include national, provincial, and pirivenas (monastic institutions). Private schools—assisted and autonomous—offer better facilities and follow the national curriculum. International schools (e.g., Edexcel, Cambridge) serve expatriate families. Tertiary education is highly competitive: only ~16% of qualified students are admitted to state universities, with admission based on A/L Z-scores and district-based representation. Top students from urban areas gain access; remote students may enter with lower marks. Unemployment among graduates remains high. Vocational education is managed by the Tertiary and Vocational Education Commission, with technical colleges, apprenticeships, and NVQSL programs. Criticisms include an overly competitive, rigid system, compulsory leadership training (ended in 2015), and lack of regulation in private degree programs.

# England
England ranks 13th globally in literacy, mathematics, and science (OECD PISA), with average scores above the OECD average. The academy system (expanded since 1997) has improved school quality, with 88% of schools rated good or outstanding by 2015. Compulsory education spans ages 5–16, with a structured National Curriculum including 13 core subjects. At Key Stage 4, students have a statutory right to study one subject from arts, design and technology, humanities, business, or a modern language. Post-16 education ends at age 16, with students required to remain in education until 18 through sixth forms, FE colleges, apprenticeships, or volunteering. Higher education includes bachelor’s (3 years, honours), integrated master’s (4 years in STEM), and postgraduate degrees (certificates to doctorates). Fees were capped at £9,535 per year from 2024–25; international students pay more. State support includes loans and bursaries, narrowing access gaps. Adult education is available via Open University and Local Education Authorities. A unified qualifications framework (RQF/FHEQ) aligns with European standards (EQF/QF-EHEA), defining levels from 1 to 8.

# Egypt
Egypt’s education system is highly centralized, with free compulsory basic education (ages 4–14). Despite high primary enrollment and low dropout rates, quality remains poor, with poor performance in international assessments (49th in reading, 34th in math). Structural issues include high student-to-teacher ratios, rote learning, and outdated pedagogies. Secondary education offers general and technical tracks, with technical education supported by the Industrial Training Council. Higher education is extensive but faces governance issues, low per-student spending, and low graduation rates (~50% of entrants graduate). The government has launched multiple reforms, including the Higher Education Enhancement Project and a Japan-inspired engineering diploma. Egypt has 184 international schools, with Cairo University at 350th and American University in Cairo at 410th in QS World University Rankings 2025.

# Ghana
Ghana’s education system is decentralized, with 16 regions and 230 district offices. The state allocates 23% of its budget to education, with significant donor funding (declined from 8.5% to 2.5% between 2005–2012). Teacher training is led by 46 Colleges of Education, offering a three-year Diploma in Basic Education (DBE), with additional pathways at universities. Adult literacy improved from 54% (1997) to 71.5% (2010) via the National Functional Literacy Programme (FNLP). Technical and vocational education (TVET) remains underdeveloped, with low completion rates and poor training. Access to tertiary education is unequal: acceptance rates dropped from 96% (2001) to 52% (2011), with women and rural students underrepresented. Socioeconomic status significantly impacts access—only 40% of female students come from the wealthiest 40%, and male students from the top quintile are over seven times more likely to attend and complete higher education than those from the poorest. Secondary education is governed by the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE), determining entry into academic or vocational tracks. Tertiary institutions use WASSCE scores (max 24 points) for admission. Private education dominates (74.7% of primary and junior secondary schools), offering smaller classes and better facilities. Governance involves the Ghana Education Service, NCCA, NaSIA, NTC, and WAEC. Challenges include teacher shortages, regional disparities, and poor alignment between curricula and labor market needs.

text:
# Indonesia
Indonesia’s education system is the fourth largest globally, with over 50 million students. Post-independence, it emphasized secular, nationalist values through Pancasila. Primary and middle school (ages 6–15) are compulsory and free, with instruction in Indonesian from the third year. High school (ages 15–18) offers academic or vocational tracks. Teacher qualifications have improved since the 1970s, and salaries are competitive in Asia. Challenges include equity, teacher shortages (especially in remote areas), funding, and low tertiary participation (36.31% in 2011). The 2013 curriculum includes specialization groups in natural sciences, social sciences, language and literature, and religion-specific tracks (e.g., Islamic, Christian). Educational levels are RA (pre-school), MI (primary), MTs (secondary), MA (senior secondary), and MAK (vocational). Higher education includes academic, vocational, and professional institutions under the Indonesian National Qualification Framework (KKNI), with levels from diploma to doctorate.

text:
# Hong Kong
Hong Kong’s education system evolved from British colonial roots to emphasize patriotism and national security post-1997. Key changes include the Target Oriented Curriculum (TOC), replacement of Liberal Studies with Citizenship and Social Development, and state-sanctioned field trips to mainland China. Textbooks have been revised to downplay colonial status and attribute protests to foreign influence. The national security law has led to declining enrolment and staff retention. Pre-school is subsidized but not free; public primary and secondary education is free and compulsory from age 6 until 18 (except those completing Form Three). Secondary education includes junior and senior years, with most schools offering the HKDSE and some providing the IB program. The commerce stream is vocational, leading to work experience or further education abroad. EMI (English Medium Instruction) schools are prestigious and have higher university acceptance rates. Tertiary education expanded significantly since the 1970s, with 8 UGC-funded universities (e.g., HKU, CUHK, HKUST) ranked globally among the top 100. Admission is primarily via JUPAS. Adult education is accessible through evening courses, vocational training, and the Open University of Hong Kong. Special education is shifting toward integration, with most special schools transitioning into mainstream settings. Immigrant and non-Cantonese-speaking children receive support via induction programs. International education is well-developed, with 175 international schools (per ISC), many offering UK or IB curricula, and high tuition fees.

# Armenia
Armenia’s education system has 100% literacy since 1960 and emphasizes national identity, history, and culture post-Soviet reform. The K–12 system includes 4 years of primary (1–4), 5 years of middle school (5–9), and 3 years of high school (10–12). Education is compulsory and free through secondary level. Public schools dominate (97%), state-funded and aligned with national standards. Entrance exams determine university or vocational school admission. The system places strong emphasis on national values. In recent years, English and Chinese language education have expanded, with the first Chinese school in Yerevan opening in 2018. Higher education is robust, with 26 state and 33 private universities, including Yerevan State University and the American University of Armenia. These institutions offer diverse programs in sciences, medicine, engineering, and humanities, with strong international recognition. Armenia is a full member of the European Higher Education Area (Bologna Process and Lisbon Recognition Convention), participates in EU mobility programs (Erasmus+), and has a quality assurance agency accredited by ENQA and EQAR. After-school centers like Tumo and SMART provide 21st-century skills. Student absenteeism and dropout rates have risen due to child labor and poor education quality.

# Sweden
Sweden’s education system includes a nine-year *grunnskole* (ages 6–16), mandatory from 1889 (7 years) to 1969 (9 years). Primary education emphasizes play-based learning and foundational skills. Lower secondary introduces grading and electives (languages or career studies), with subject-specific exams. Students perform well internationally (OECD PISA 2009), though math performance lags behind Shanghai. Upper secondary education includes two main types: preparatory (leading to university eligibility) and vocational (job-specific skills). In 2024–2025, two-thirds of students enroll in preparatory programs (e.g., Social Science, Natural Science, Business Management), and one-third in vocational ones (e.g., Health, Construction, Tourism). All students take core courses in English, Swedish, math, and civic education, plus a diploma project requiring planning, execution, and reflection. Eligibility requires passing 12 (preparatory) or 8 (vocational) subjects, with 3 core subjects mandatory. Students failing to qualify may enter introductory programs. Higher education includes academic degrees (bachelor’s, master’s, PhD) through public universities and university colleges, with degrees following the Bologna Process (180, 120, 240 credits). Higher education is free for Swedish, EU/EEA, and Swiss citizens. Independent schools (friskolor) have grown significantly and spark debate over equity, quality, and profit motives.

# Norway
Norway’s education system has roots dating back to 2000 B.C., with formal schooling beginning as cathedral schools after 1153. Post-Reformation, Latin schools became mandatory in market towns. Compulsory reading was introduced in 1736, and the *folkeskole* became mandatory from 1889 (7 years), expanded to 9 years in 1969, and later replaced by the *grunnskole* (ages 6–16). The system includes elementary (6–12), lower secondary (13–16), and upper secondary (16–19). Primary school emphasizes play-based learning; lower secondary introduces grading and electives. Students perform well internationally (OECD PISA 2009), though math performance lags behind Shanghai. Upper secondary education is mostly public (93% in 2007), with a 1994 reform unifying general, mercantile, and vocational tracks into a flexible system. The *Kunnskapsløftet* (2006) emphasizes general knowledge and allows transitions between paths. Vocational programs follow a "2+2" model (2 years of school, 2 years of apprenticeship), while general studies focus on theory. Graduation rates are at 73% (2017). Teachers are categorized by level: *førskolelærer* (preschool), *adjunkt* (bachelor’s, grades 5–10), and *lektor* (master’s, upper secondary). Higher education requires *generell studiekompetanse* , typically earned through general studies or via age/work experience. Most institutions are state-run, with quality assured by NOKUT. Private schools are limited and must offer internationally recognized curricula or religious/pedagogical alternatives, with strict government oversight and no ability-based selection.

# Higher Education Framework (Common Across Nations)
All systems feature a structured progression from primary to tertiary education, with increasing emphasis on national identity, equity, and international competitiveness. Key features include national exams, standardized curricula, and a mix of public and private institutions. Admission to higher education often depends on performance in national or regional exams. Vocational and academic pathways are increasingly integrated, with many countries moving toward blended models. Teacher training, quality assurance, and digital integration are central to reform efforts. Challenges remain in teacher shortages, curriculum modernization, labor market alignment, and gender disparities. Despite regional differences, a shared trend toward inclusivity, equity, and global engagement defines modern education systems in these countries.
